Content-gap review: 2026-11-27

Owner-approved additions for browser and computer-use agents, A2A peers, developer workstations, and skill and plugin supply chain. Existing items were extended; no item was added and no ID or gate changed.

GapResult
Browser and computer-use agentsRun-time rule 1 lists screen, DOM, and download inputs (S68, S69). Build-time rule 5 names form submission, purchases, uploads, downloads, and accepting terms (S68, S69). Build-time rule 8 adds a separate browser VM or profile without personal logins; Build-time rule 9 adds a browser domain allowlist; Run-time rule 13 adds step logs and screenshots.
A2A peersEcosystem rule 7 gains protocol specifics verified against A2A 1.0.0 (S70): TLS (§7.1), JWS-signed Agent Cards over JCS (§8.4), out-of-band credentials in headers (§7.3, §7.6.3), TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED is not authorization (§7.6.4), webhook SSRF checks and notification authentication (§4.3.3, §13.2). Ecosystem rule 8 counts remote A2A tasks as delegation.
Developer workstationsBuild-time rule 2, Build-time rule 8, and Build-time rule 12 cover personal credentials, sandboxes or devcontainers, managed settings, and auto-approved project MCP servers (S71, S72). S72 warns that a devcontainer does not protect credentials stored inside it.
Skill and plugin supply chainEcosystem rule 2 and Ecosystem rule 3 treat skills, plugins, hooks, and extensions as code: review, pinning, auto-update, and marketplace allowlists (S73, with incident evidence S62 and S64).

The vendor documents describe one product each. BRACE generalizes their precautions; it doesn't claim every product offers the same controls.

Latest review: 2026-10-22

The full dated evidence review rechecks all 53 items and recipes, with a row for every item, original advisory links, affected/fixed versions, configuration prerequisites and source limits. Newly published October 19–21 advisories are distinguished from older omissions found now. This is a source review, not a dependency audit, exploit reproduction, model requalification or deployment test.

Approved policy clarification: high-stakes or high-autonomy deployments receive evidence, gaps and unknowns, without a BRACE GO/NO-GO deployment verdict. Unrated deployments also receive findings only. Accountable people own any deployment decision and a gradual, closely monitored rollout with bounded exposure, stop conditions, tested recovery and review before expansion. Lower-risk GO/NO-GO results describe checklist record conditions, not deployment authorization. This supersedes earlier release-approval wording below; government guidance recommends low-risk, non-sensitive uses and does not endorse a high-risk release after BRACE gates pass.

Rechecked concernFinding and discussion implication
Patching versus configured remediationMCP TypeScript/Python issuer, audience and validation fixes can require explicit settings, stored-credential cleanup and application lifecycle changes. A patched version alone is insufficient evidence.
Inputs before inferenceOctober 20 vLLM advisories cover media decoder dispatch, GPU exhaustion, token ranges and unauthenticated browser-reachable endpoints. Token budgets and prompt checks do not cover every preprocessing failure.
Persistent authority and influenceHook registration, files, summaries and handoffs can change later execution. Namespace encoding and batch/async/auth-hook paths need concrete isolation tests.
Verification and recoveryA missed August Cosign advisory concerns legacy blob bundles, explicitly not OCI images. Checkpoint object revival and model-loader advisories distinguish authenticity from safe decoding.
Metadata and scanningFingerprinting all reviewed metadata and containing scanner startup are distinct from scanning descriptions. Skills over MCP adds host-specific activation, origin and cache boundaries.
Shutdown and evidenceCooperative cancellation does not prove execution has stopped. Complete action evidence should retain necessary detail in protected storage without leaking secrets into normal logs.
Standards and assurance claimsMCP versioning still identifies 2026-07-28; identity drafts and OTel Development conventions retain their stated limits. BRACE's exact schema, context metric and priorities remain design judgments.

Apart from the approved release-policy clarification, these technical refinements remain discussion inputs. They have not silently changed checklist controls, gates or existing model qualification claims. Updated references are indexed in the resource catalog.

Conclusion and limits

The core control approach is consistent with the primary guidance reviewed, subject to the corrections below. All 53 requirements and their verification recipes were reviewed for practical accuracy using the available documentation. This is not a deployment test, product certification, or proof that these controls prevent every attack. Effectiveness must be demonstrated on the actual release using the verification recipes.

Before the initial 2026-09-16 review, the source inventory contained 70 distinct external URLs. The initial link check successfully retrieved 67 sources (HTTP 200); three blocked access (HTTP 403). A successful response establishes reachability, not accuracy or implementation effectiveness. Relevant primary documentation was then read to check the security claims and catalog descriptions; the inventory states the verification limits for other references. Product source code, all linked subpages, and proprietary service internals were not comprehensively audited.

The nine controls, exact six-field identity schema, decision-time context requirement, top-three selections, and release gates are BRACE design judgments. Sources support related principles; they do not prescribe this exact checklist or validate its ranking. Mappings to standards show related concepts; they do not establish compliance.

Findings and corrections

FindingCorrection and practical consequence
Revocation is not universally immediate.Build-time rule 4 now requires a measured revocation time limit appropriate to the potential harm covering existing sessions and self-contained/cached tokens. RFC 7009 describes propagation considerations; disabling refresh alone is insufficient.
Approval can be replayed or become stale.Build-time rule 5/B06 now bind authorization to operation, target, and arguments, check relevant state at execution, and test concurrent replay. See OWASP transaction authorization.
Network allowlists and signatures can be overclaimed.Build-time rule 9 includes redirect/DNS and allowed-service abuse. Build-time rule 10 requires an approved signing identity as well as digest verification. Build-time rule 11 distinguishes sandbox architecture from a few successful denial probes.
Input validation is not a complete prompt-injection defense.Run-time rule 1/R02 retain separate structural validation, treatment of external text as data, and independently enforced action permissions. Run-time rule 3 also covers generated content consumed by interpreters. See OWASP injection prevention.
Context and remote implementation identity can be unobservable.Run-time rule 7 records counting method and uncertainty. Ecosystem rule 3 distinguishes metadata hashes from hidden remote implementation changes. Model and training records now identify unavailable details explicitly.
Integrity and replay claims need stronger assumptions.Run-time rule 14 requires independently protected trust state and scoped destination idempotency guarantees, or a manual reconciliation hold. Stripe’s documented behavior is a concrete example, not a guarantee for other integrations.
An HTTP gateway does not cover every MCP transport.Ecosystem rule 6 and the gateway guide distinguish OAuth/HTTP authorization from host/process/sandbox controls for local stdio. See MCP authorization.
Existing OpenTelemetry coverage was understated.Current GenAI conventions already include agent identity/version and agent/tool spans. BRACE’s extra fields are labeled custom proposals; context propagation must be instrumented and verified. Agent spans remain Development.
Framework novelty and vendor rankings were unsupported.Added OWASP ACS, removed sweeping exclusivity claims, and replaced product checkmarks/rankings with an evidence worksheet. The Microsoft gateway reference is a draft with conformance requirements, not proof of independent conformance testing.
Catalog maintenance and lifecycle claims had drifted.Marked Daytona and LLM Guard repositories as unmaintained; recorded Guardrails migration and Snyk Agent Scan experimental-output limitations.
OpenAI lifecycle wording exceeded the source.Agent Builder docs state a November 30, 2026 sunset and that ChatKit continues. Removed the unsupported Evals sunset claim and claims that vendors do not version workflows.
A study result was easy to overgeneralize.The 73.5% debugging/logging figure describes vulnerabilities identified in the sampled skill study, not all agent vulnerabilities in the wild.

Update review: 2026-09-30

All 53 checklist items and their recipes were rechecked against guidance published or revised since the first review. The 2026-09-30 review changed 36 checklist items and 37 recipes, plus the model provenance table; it added no items and changed no gates. Each quote below was read from the primary source on 2026-09-30 unless marked otherwise.

FindingCorrection and practical consequence
MCP 2026-07-28 replaced 2025-11-25 as the current protocol version.S3/S4 now cite 2026-07-28. Ecosystem rule 6 adds header/body mismatch rejection ("MUST reject requests where the values specified in the headers do not match"), caching keyed by authorization context, and iss validation. Without them, a gateway that routes on Mcp-Name can authorize one tool while the body calls another. Ecosystem rule 9 and Run-time rule 11 replace "tool sessions", which 2026-07-28 removed, with streams, subscriptions, and tasks.
MCP metadata beyond descriptions reaches the model; annotations and serverInfo are self-reported.Ecosystem rule 4 scans server instructions, annotations, and templates. Build-time rule 1 no longer lets annotations drive allow/approval decisions ("untrusted unless they come from trusted servers"). Ecosystem rule 5 stops deriving identity from serverInfo.name ("not guaranteed to be unique"). Ecosystem rule 3 stops serving cached definitions after a failed re-check. See S19 and S20.
Current guidance recommends a design-level rule on capability combinations.Build-time rule 5, a Blocker item, now treats every consequential action as high-impact when one context combines untrusted input, sensitive access, and external action (S21), unless an isolation pattern from S22 applies. An agent could previously pass every item while holding all three with no approval.
Single-attempt injection tests overstate robustness.The Run-time rule 2 recipe now repeats fixtures and adds adaptive variants. S23 reports hijack success rising from 57% to 80% at 25 attempts.
Rendered output and memory self-promotion were uncovered exfiltration and persistence paths.Run-time rule 3 covers auto-fetched URLs in rendered Markdown. Run-time rule 5 blocks unreviewed promotion of agent output, expires unverified entries, and tests query-only poisoning (S24).
Bearer tokens, audience, push revocation, and delegation chains were underspecified.Build-time rule 2 adds audience restriction; Build-time rule 3 sender-constrained tokens (S25); Build-time rule 4 push revocation (S26). Build-time rule 6 binds approval to the requesting instance and records approver and expiry (S1: "Include the actor … and expiry"). Ecosystem rule 8 adds per-hop downscoping and ignores prior actors (S27: "informational only"). Agent rule 4 records the delegated subject.
The IETF agent-auth draft moved to a working group.draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03 is "Replaced by draft-ietf-wimse-aims" (S28, revision -00, 15 September 2026). Catalog links updated. It is an Internet-Draft, not an RFC.
Signature checks could pass without provenance, enforcement scope, or a patched verifier.Build-time rule 10 verifies builder, source, and parameters (S9), and requires enforcing mode on production namespaces. It also requires a cosign release fixed for GHSA-whqx-f9j3-ch6m (patched in 2.6.2 and 3.0.4; S29). Build-time rule 11 names a container baseline (S30). Build-time rule 12 protects source history.
Model files lacked signer and serialization checks; hosted IDs were classified by naming alone.Configuration rule 5, Configuration rule 3, Configuration rule 4, and the new provenance row require signed weights and adapters, verified before load (S31, S32). Configuration rule 1 classifies IDs from provider documentation. Anthropic IDs from the 4.6 generation on are dateless pinned snapshots, while earlier dateless IDs are aliases, and "serving infrastructure … can change over time" (S33). Configuration rule 7 checks that hosted recovery models are still served.
The stop path and audit capture could depend on the agent.Run-time rule 11 requires a stop path outside the agent's credentials and tests an attempt to disable it. Ecosystem rule 10 covers log deletion requested through tools (S34: "Quarantine requests to delete logs or audit records"). Ecosystem rule 11 fails closed ("Fail closed when … audit logging fails", S1) and sets retention by law (S35). Run-time rule 13 records policy version and approval ID.
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions changed after the first review.S14 is pinned to commit b9ecbae (30 September 2026); status remains Development. Run-time rule 7 references gen_ai.conversation.compacted. Agent rule 2 rejects identity from baggage, which has "no built-in integrity checks". Agent rule 6 notes that prompt capture is opt-in.
An AI-specific incident-response source was missing.Ecosystem rule 12 adds a named reporting decision. See S36 and S37.

Not verified in the 2026-09-30 review:

  • The ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, and 27001 pages block scripted retrieval; each was confirmed in a browser on 2026-09-30 (42001:2023 and 23894:2023, both Edition 1; 27001:2022). The full paywalled texts were not reviewed.
  • The OWASP ASI01–ASI10 identifiers appear only in the downloadable document, not on the landing page.

These limits do not change any requirement.

Targeted MCP update: 2026-10-16

This update reviews MCP credential/delegation language, gateway deployment patterns, tool publication, protocol state/extensions, and the related verification recipes. It is not a new audit of every external reference, an exhaustive literature review, or a deployment/conformance test. Existing evaluation snapshots and historical outreach remain records of their evaluated versions. Changing the review checks requires fresh model qualification; historical model results do not validate this revision.

FindingRevision and evidence
An access token need not represent only a service account.Build-time rule 2/B03 and the guides distinguish acting-agent identity from machine or explicitly delegated user/system authority. Gateway and backend audiences are checked separately. Supported exchange is an option, not an issuer capability every backend has. S3, S27, S41, S42.
An internal network design was described too broadly.Ecosystem rule 6 and the gateway guide distinguish internal HTTP, public third-party and local stdio enforcement. Private networks and mTLS are one internal pattern. Public services need effective controls over agent egress and credential custody; local processes need host/sandbox restrictions. S4, S43, S44.
Tool discovery and publication need distinct states.Ecosystem rule 3 adds disabled discovery, owner approval, versioned grants, bounded config propagation, quarantine and rollback that preserves revocations. Uber's reports support the pattern; they are not independent verification or normative MCP requirements. S45, S46.
Policy can be bypassed through alternate invocation paths.Ecosystem rule 6 and its recipe cover direct, dynamic, wrapper and CLI/code-mode calls, with operation/resource/tenant/argument checks. The protocol does not itself enforce the approved business task. S44, S46, S47.
New protocol state and extensions need explicit ownership.Ecosystem rule 6 and Configuration rule 1 record protocol/extension versions, private cache isolation, task/state-handle authorization, Tasks cancellation and Apps host controls. 2026-07-28 removed protocol sessions; older clients still need their applicable binding tests. Self-reported metadata is not identity. S19, S43, S48.
A clean scan can be mistaken for sufficient assurance.Recipes require allowed-task results and concrete denial/outage tests. The research catalog distinguishes benchmark results, demonstrations, empirical scanner studies and proposed defenses. No cross-study attack rate or certification claim is made. S49–S57.
Guidance and specifications have different authority.The catalog labels protocol requirements, RFCs, optional stable/draft extensions, CoSAI profiles, project-specific gateway specifications, deployment reports and research. MCP authorization is optional at protocol level; BRACE requires it for protected access. CoSAI assurance profiles are additional requirements when adopted, not automatic BRACE certification. S3, S16, S41–S43, S48.

The targeted source set is listed in the MCP resource catalog, including original Invariant, Trail of Bits, JFrog and Pillar disclosures. These reports have different attacker assumptions and dates. We did not reproduce exploits, independently audit vendor systems, or re-run published benchmarks.

Evidence still unavailable

  • Public metadata for ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 23894 was inspected, but the full paywalled standards were not. No clause-level completeness or compliance conclusion is claimed.
  • Vendor feature coverage, configuration defaults, deployment performance, and security effectiveness require version-specific evidence and testing. The vendor worksheet records what to request rather than assigning unsupported passes.
  • Historical outreach drafts are marked as historical; their novelty statements are not current verified claims.

Incident evidence added 2026-11-26 (brace-dgo.2). Each is vendor- or researcher-reported and was read at the source on 2026-11-26. They illustrate failure modes; they do not change any requirement.

  • S60: Botpress security incident disclosure (2026-11-06). A flawed sign-in proxy let an attacker read bot configurations in 16 workspaces; those can hold third-party credentials, including AI provider keys. Botpress asks customers to treat every stored credential as exposed.
  • S61: Railway October security incident report (2026-11-10). A build-isolation escape, a build credential trusted by an internal service, and a misconfigured OIDC binding led to a long-lived decryption credential. Environment variables were decrypted for at most 1.85% of workspaces.
  • S62: Cursor security incident update (2026-11-13). A storage key issued to an inference provider was exposed; stored coding-agent traces held some unredacted credentials, which reached internal SaaS tools. A stolen credential also placed a tampered extension on the marketplace cache.
  • S63: LiteLLM attack-chain analysis (2026-10-23). An admin key committed in May was never revoked. It exposed an owner's GitHub token, then CI secrets, a changed release workflow and a malicious litellm==1.107.0.
  • S64: Cursor notice on the tampered Claude Code extension (2026-10-29, updated 2026-10-30). Versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, not built by Anthropic, were in the Cursor marketplace for about 11 hours. The notice gives no user count.
  • S65: Symantec, unauthorized relays for Codex and Claude Code (2026-10-29). A setup script rewrites the CLIs' config files: Codex sandbox set to full access, base URLs and keys pointed at a relay. Not a product vulnerability; abuse not observed.
  • S66: Pillar Security, opencode RCE via MCP OAuth (byline 2026-10-19). A remote MCP server's authorization_endpoint reached an unescaped launcher on Windows and WSL. Fixed in opencode 1.18.33; no CVE published.
  • S67: Straiker, session inception (2026-10-08). A child CLI session started in an untrusted repository ran the repository's hook without the parent's confirmation. The vendor closed the report as Informative.
  • S68: Anthropic, computer use tool: security considerations (checked 2026-11-27). Recommends a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges, no account logins, a domain allowlist, and human confirmation for consequential actions. Warns that instructions on web pages or in images can override the user's.
  • S69: OpenAI, computer use guide (checked 2026-11-27). "Treat screen content as untrusted"; use an isolated browser or VM, a fresh profile, network rules, and confirmation for purchases, data transmission, and destructive changes.
  • S70: A2A Protocol Specification 1.0.0 (checked 2026-11-27). TLS required in production, TLS 1.3 recommended (§7.1); optional JWS Agent Card signatures over JCS, which clients SHOULD verify (§8.4); out-of-band credentials (§7.3); auth-required state is not authorization (§7.6.4); webhook SSRF checks and authentication (§13.2). Signing is optional, so many cards will be unsigned.
  • S71: Claude Code settings and settings reference (checked 2026-11-27). Managed settings (file, MDM, or server-managed) override user and project files. enableAllProjectMcpServers approves every server in a project .mcp.json without a prompt; allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, and strictKnownMarketplaces are managed-only controls.
  • S72: Claude Code development containers (checked 2026-11-27). With permission checks skipped, a devcontainer does not stop a malicious project from exfiltrating anything inside it, including Claude Code's credentials; avoid mounting ~/.ssh or cloud credential files. Policy in a repository Dockerfile can be changed by anyone with write access.
  • S73: Claude Code plugin security and trust (checked 2026-11-27). Plugins can run arbitrary code with user privileges; hooks, monitors, and MCP servers run outside the sandbox; auto-update can change reviewed files; commit-SHA and sha256 pins and managed marketplace allowlists are available.

Each row records the practical issue checked or clarified. An unchanged item means no design correction was identified in this review; it does not mean an implementation has passed. Use the linked verification guide for procedures and expected evidence.

Agent rule 2S11 S14 S13The exact six fields are a BRACE schema choice; verify completeness on asynchronous and failed actions too.
Agent rule 3S9Canonical manifest hashing is a BRACE design; opaque model references identify recorded provenance, not invisible weights.
Agent rule 4S3 S13 S27 S28Trace labels are correlation data, not authentication; derive authoritative identity in a trusted layer.
Agent rule 5S1 S11Exercise the operator lookup and targeted containment procedure.
Agent rule 6S1 S14 S14Check nested lineage and authorized retrieval of protected prompts; account for retention and privacy.
Agent rule 7S1 S14Inventory auxiliary and routing models too; declare provider-hidden details as unknown.
Configuration rule 1S9 S17 S33Manifest must explicitly name model/checkpoint/adapter and training provenance where available; do not invent unavailable provider internals.
Configuration rule 3S9 S32Compare deployment evidence to the manifest; managed aliases limit proof of immutable model identity.
Configuration rule 4S1 S9 S32 S65Exercise drift detection and its response; versioned storage alone does not prove the running state.
Configuration rule 2S1 S9Require review for changes that affect authority, inputs, models, or behavior.
Configuration rule 5S1 S9 S31 S32 S33 S63Explicitly track model, adapter, training-run, and data-reference changes as well as software dependencies.
Configuration rule 6S1 S2 S34Use deployment-specific regression and injection cases; a passing finite suite is bounded evidence.
Configuration rule 7S1 S9 S12 S33Test restart and rollback with state compatibility; a code rollback cannot undo committed external effects.
Configuration rule 8S11 S14Verify retained trace-to-release and prompt references; the exact BRACE join is custom instrumentation.
Ecosystem rule 6S3 S4 S16 S19 S20 S43 S44 S47 S48Apply HTTP authorization or equivalent local stdio enforcement as appropriate; cover bypass and response paths.
Ecosystem rule 8S1 S3 S27 S70Exercise privilege escalation through a peer; delegation must not bypass the caller’s authorization.
Ecosystem rule 9S1Prove the stop reaches remote descendants, queues, credentials, and retries within the chosen budget.
Ecosystem rule 1S1 S15Assign platform and team responsibilities; an upstream product claim is not implementation evidence.
Ecosystem rule 2S1 S8 S9 S20 S31 S63 S64 S66 S73Pin observable artifacts, assess maintenance, and record remote implementation limitations.
Ecosystem rule 3S4 S16 S19 S20 S46 S66 S73Metadata fingerprints detect metadata changes; they cannot attest hidden remote code.
Ecosystem rule 4S2 S4 S19 S20 S49 S53Scan metadata with a failure policy; scanners have false positives and evasion limits.
Ecosystem rule 5S3 S4 S19Bind server identity plus tool name; names alone do not establish provenance.
Ecosystem rule 7S1 S6 S20 S70Authenticate, authorize, validate, and prevent replay of action-bearing peer messages.
Ecosystem rule 10S11 S13 S14 S34Verify cross-service propagation and protected evidence; standards do not guarantee instrumentation completeness.
Ecosystem rule 11S11 S1 S35 S62Test retention, access, export, loss detection, and safe behavior when audit capture fails.
Ecosystem rule 12S1 S15 S34 S36 S37Run a shared-dependency incident drill with affected-instance discovery and accountable responders.

Reverification policy

Repeat source/lifecycle checks when adopting or upgrading a dependency and when a linked draft changes. Repeat applicable checklist tests on the deployed release after security-relevant changes. Retain dated evidence, version identifiers, known visibility limits, and an owner for unresolved gaps; a source’s continued availability does not keep a prior test result current.
